title: Biomedical Signals and Systems
description: Biomedical Signals and Systems teaches students to model, acquire, process, analyze, and interpret physiological signals using signals-and-systems theory and biomedical engineering judgment.

topics.title: Continuous- and discrete-time signals
topics.description: This opening section gives students the language for describing signals before any filtering or analysis begins. The goal is to see physiological measurements as structured data: waveforms with units, timing, amplitude, morphology, and sampling choices.

children.title: Signal representations
children.description: Students learn to distinguish continuous waveforms from sampled sequences and to describe each with appropriate notation.

children.title: Independent variable, amplitude, units, duration, and sampling index
Deterministic, random, periodic, aperiodic, energy, and power signals
Biomedical waveform examples
children.description: The abstract notation is connected to real signals students will analyze later.

children.title: ECG Voltage Traces and Cardiac Cycles
EMG Bursts, PPG Pulses, Pressure Traces, and Respiratory Signals
Basic operations on signals
children.description: Operations help students model alignment, scaling, normalization, and comparison of recordings.

children.title: Time shifting, scaling, reversal, and windowing
Amplitude scaling, baseline removal, and normalization
Measurement context
children.description: Students learn that signals are shaped by physiology, sensors, and data-acquisition choices.

children.title: Artifacts from motion, electrode contact, mains interference, and physiology outside the target system

topics.title: Linear time-invariant systems
topics.description: LTI systems provide the central model for many filters, sensors, and simplified physiological subsystems. The point is not that every biological process is linear, but that linear models are powerful approximations when used carefully.

children.title: Linearity and superposition
children.description: Students learn when outputs can be decomposed into responses to simpler inputs.

children.title: Where biomedical systems are locally linear
Limits of linear approximations in saturation, thresholds, and nonlinear physiology
Time invariance
children.description: This concept clarifies whether a system behaves the same way at different times.

children.title: Examples from filters, amplifiers, and physiological regulation
System properties
children.description: Students learn the vocabulary for judging system behavior before solving equations.

children.title: Biomedical system models
children.description: The course connects LTI thinking to real measurement and physiology.

children.title: Respiratory, cardiovascular, and neural response models
Filter blocks in bedside monitors and wearable devices

topics.title: Convolution and impulse response
topics.description: Convolution explains how an input waveform is transformed by a system with memory. For biomedical engineering, it is the bridge between physical measurement chains, filtering, and interpretation of delayed or smeared signals.

children.title: Impulse response meaning
children.description: Students learn that the impulse response is a complete description of an LTI system.

children.title: Biomedical examples such as sensor response time and hemodynamic response
Convolution mechanics
children.description: Students practice the operation visually, analytically, and computationally.

children.title: System memory and smoothing
children.description: Convolution reveals why filters smooth, delay, or spread signal features.

children.title: Applications to physiological data
children.description: Students use convolution to interpret realistic waveform processing.

children.title: ECG Smoothing and QRS Morphology Effects
Impulse-like events in neural or muscular recordings

topics.title: Fourier series and Fourier transforms
topics.description: This section teaches students to analyze signals by frequency content. The point is to recognize rhythms, bandwidth, noise sources, and periodic structure that may be hidden in the time-domain trace.

children.title: Frequency-domain intuition
children.description: Students learn what a spectrum says about a signal.

children.title: Fourier series
children.description: Students represent periodic signals as sums of harmonically related sinusoids.

children.title: Examples from cardiac and respiratory cycles
Fourier transform
children.description: Students extend frequency analysis to nonperiodic or finite-duration signals.

children.title: Fast Fourier Transform as a Computational Tool
Biomedical spectral analysis
children.description: Students connect spectra to physiological interpretation.

children.title: EMG Median Frequency and Fatigue Analysis

topics.title: Sampling, aliasing, and reconstruction
topics.description: Sampling determines what information enters the digital record. Students learn how to choose sampling rates, avoid aliasing, and understand when reconstruction from samples is mathematically and practically credible.

children.title: Sampling theorem
children.description: Students learn the core requirement for preserving signal frequency content.

children.title: Aliasing
children.description: Students learn how high-frequency content can masquerade as lower-frequency content.

children.title: Why anti-alias filtering matters before digitization
Quantization and ADC basics
children.description: Students connect sampling to data-acquisition hardware.

children.title: Bit Depth, Resolution, and Dynamic Range
Reconstruction and interpolation
children.description: Students understand what can and cannot be recovered from sampled data.

children.title: Resampling, decimation, and synchronization across channels

topics.title: Laplace and z-transform methods
topics.description: Transforms give compact ways to analyze dynamic systems, filters, and stability. The goal is to make differential and difference equations usable for design and interpretation.

children.title: Laplace transform foundations
children.description: Students learn to solve and interpret continuous-time system behavior.

children.title: Transform pairs and regions of convergence
Z-transform foundations
children.description: Students learn the discrete-time analogue needed for digital filters.

children.title: Poles, zeros, and stability
children.description: Students use pole-zero structure to predict system behavior.

children.title: Stability criteria in continuous and discrete domains
Biomedical modeling uses
children.description: Students apply transform methods to realistic signal and system questions.

topics.title: Digital filter design
topics.description: Filtering is one of the most practical skills in biomedical signal analysis. Students learn to remove noise and artifacts without destroying the signal features that matter physiologically or clinically.

children.title: Filter specifications
children.description: Students learn to define what a filter must do before choosing a method.

children.title: Passband, stopband, cutoff, ripple, and attenuation
Low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, band-stop, and notch filters
Biomedical Constraints Such as Preserving ECG QRS Morphology
FIR and IIR filters
children.description: Students compare major digital filter families.

children.title: Butterworth, Chebyshev, and Elliptic IIR Designs
Implementation effects
children.description: Students learn that filter equations have practical consequences.

children.title: Biomedical filtering cases
children.description: Students apply filters to common physiological recordings.

topics.title: Time-frequency analysis
topics.description: Many biomedical signals change over time, so a single spectrum can hide important dynamics. This section helps students analyze transient events, bursts, changing rhythms, and state transitions.

children.title: Short-time Fourier transform
children.description: Students learn the basic windowed approach to changing spectra.

children.title: Wavelet concepts
children.description: Students learn why multiscale methods are useful for transient biomedical signals.

children.title: Event-related analysis
children.description: Students connect time-frequency tools to physiological events.

children.title: Practical interpretation
children.description: Students learn to avoid over-reading colorful plots.

topics.title: Noise reduction and feature extraction
topics.description: This section turns signal processing into usable measurements. Students learn to clean data, detect meaningful events, and extract features that can support physiology, device testing, or clinical decision support.

children.title: Noise and artifact taxonomy
children.description: Students learn to identify what kind of contamination they are dealing with.

children.title: Mains interference, muscle artifacts, and sensor drift
Denoising strategies
children.description: Students compare methods for improving signal quality.

children.title: Artifact rejection, interpolation, and robust preprocessing
Feature extraction
children.description: Students learn how waveforms become quantitative descriptors.

children.title: Amplitude, area, slope, and morphology features
Spectral power, entropy, and variability features
Validation and uncertainty
children.description: Students learn that extracted features need evidence.

children.title: Reproducibility, missing data, and patient variability

topics.title: Physiological signal analysis project
topics.description: The project pulls the course together through a realistic workflow. Students select or receive a physiological dataset, define an analysis question, process the data, validate their choices, and communicate results responsibly.

children.title: Project framing
children.description: Students learn to turn a biomedical recording into an answerable engineering question.

children.title: Analysis pipeline
children.description: Students build a transparent sequence from raw data to results.

children.title: Evaluation
children.description: Students test whether their analysis is credible.

children.title: Comparison against annotations or expected physiology
Error analysis and sensitivity to parameter choices
Communication
children.description: Students practice explaining both engineering methods and biomedical meaning.
